Extract Months and Years from Order Date

# Convert order date with day first
df['Order Date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['Order Date'], dayfirst=True)

# Create month and year columns
df['Sale Year'] = df['Order Date'].dt.year
df['Sale Month'] = df['Order Date'].dt.month

# Verify it worked
print(df[['Order Date', 'Sale Year', 'Sale Month']].head(10))
print("Missing years:", df['Sale Year'].isna().sum())
print("Missing months:", df['Sale Month'].isna().sum())

Getting into the Data

# Sums sales by month and year
sales_summary = df.groupby(['Sale Year', 'Sale Month']).agg(
    total_sales=('Sales', 'sum')
).reset_index()

# Sorts by year and month
sales_summary = sales_summary.sort_values(['Sale Year', 'Sale Month']).reset_index(drop=True)

# Sort years and months
years = sorted(sales_summary['Sale Year'].unique())
months = np.arange(1, 13)

bar_width = 0.8 / len(years)

# Loop through the years
for i, year in enumerate(years):
    
    yearly_data = sales_summary[sales_summary['Sale Year'] == year]
    
    # Go through month by month
    sales_by_month = []
    
    for month in months:
        value = yearly_data[yearly_data['Sale Month'] == month]['total_sales']
        
        # Check if data exists
        if len(value) > 0:
            #Return value
            sales_by_month.append(value.values[0])
        else:
            #Return 0
            sales_by_month.append(0)
    
    # Plot bars
    plt.bar(
        months + i * bar_width,
        sales_by_month,
        width=bar_width,
        label=str(year)
    )

# Add labels
plt.xlabel('Month')
plt.ylabel('Total Sales')
plt.title('Monthly Sales by Year')

# Center x-axis labels
plt.xticks(
    months + bar_width * (len(years) - 1) / 2,
    months
)

# Add legend and gridlines
plt.legend(title='Year')
plt.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3)

plt.show()

There is a clear pattern over the years of sales being lowest at the beginning of the year, in January and February, then building through the year and spiking in September, November, and December.

# Get yearly totals
yearly_sales = sales_summary.groupby('Sale Year', as_index=False).agg(
    total_sales=('total_sales', 'sum')
)

# Graph sales by year
plt.bar(
    yearly_sales['Sale Year'],
    yearly_sales['total_sales']
)

# Add labels
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Total Sales')
plt.title('Total Sales by Year')

# Add gridlines and set tick marks
plt.xticks(yearly_sales['Sale Year'], yearly_sales['Sale Year'])
plt.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3)

plt.show()

The business shows year over year growth, going from under $500,000 in 2015 to over $700,000 in 2018. That’s an increase of over 50%.

# Get totals by state
state_sales = df.groupby('State', as_index=False).agg(
    total_sales=('Sales', 'sum')
).sort_values('total_sales', ascending=False)

# Only include top 10 selling states
top_states = state_sales.head(10)

# Graph top 10 states
plt.barh(
    top_states['State'],
    top_states['total_sales']
)

# Add labels
plt.xlabel('Total Sales')
plt.ylabel('State')
plt.title('Total Sales by State')

# Put highest at top and add gridlines
plt.gca().invert_yaxis()
plt.grid(axis='x', alpha=0.3)

plt.show()

California leads the way in total sales, with New York, Texas, Washington, and Pennsylvania rounding out the top five. All five states have over $100,000 in sales.

# Get totals by sub category
subcat_sales = df.groupby('Sub-Category', as_index=False).agg(
    total_sales=('Sales', 'sum')
).sort_values('total_sales', ascending=False)

# Graph sales by sub category
plt.barh(
    subcat_sales['Sub-Category'],
    subcat_sales['total_sales']
)

# Add labels
plt.xlabel('Total Sales')
plt.ylabel('Sub-Category')
plt.title('Total Sales by Subcategories')

# Put highest at top and add gridlines
plt.gca().invert_yaxis()
plt.grid(axis='x', alpha=0.3)

plt.show()

Phones take the top spot in sales with over $300,000. The next three, chairs, storage, and tables, are all in the furniture category showing furnitures importance for overall sales.

# Get order volume by ship mode
ship_volume = df.groupby('Ship Mode', as_index=False).agg(
    order_count=('Order ID', 'count')
).sort_values('order_count', ascending=False)

# Graph order volume by ship mode
plt.bar(
    ship_volume['Ship Mode'],
    ship_volume['order_count'],
)

# Add labels
plt.xlabel('Ship Mode')
plt.ylabel('Number of Orders')
plt.title('Order Volume by Ship Mode')
plt.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3)

plt.show()

Standard shipping makes up the majority of orders with the number of orders decreasing as the cost of the shipping method increases.

# Convert ship date and calculate fulfillment days
df['Ship Date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['Ship Date'], dayfirst=True)
df['fulfillment_days'] = (df['Ship Date'] - df['Order Date']).dt.days

# Box plot of fulfillment days by ship mode
plt.boxplot(
    [df[df['Ship Mode'] == mode]['fulfillment_days'] for mode in df['Ship Mode'].unique()],
    labels=df['Ship Mode'].unique(),
    patch_artist=True
)

# Add labels
plt.xlabel('Ship Mode')
plt.ylabel('Days to Ship')
plt.title('Order-to-Ship Time by Ship Mode')
plt.grid(axis='y', alpha=0.3)

plt.show()

As expected, standard class shipping had the longest order to ship time with an average of 5 days. Second class had an average of 3 days, first class had an average of 2 days, and same day on average was true to its name.
